
=================================================================
#65 Descent  (657 September)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: sabi · tone: clan face-off (shonen)
Logline: Eight grudges, forty-one sons, and not one loyalty he didn’t create by decree.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: Nightmares ──
[1] ¶ He starts dreaming about the Rock of Politics. In the dream it is dry, and he is rubbing it with brine, and the brine will not stay. Every time he lifts the cloth the stone is dry again, and the eight elders are standing round it waiting for it to sweat.
[2] ¶ Some nights it is the white deer, come back out of the dark it was kept in, and too big for the hunting ground. Some nights it is a boat on the water with a man sitting very straight in the stern, not rowing, counting.
[3] King Euija: (waking, to the dark) Who’s counting? / …Who’s there. Light. Somebody bring a light!
[4] The Court Maids: Majesty. It’s only us. / …You were saying numbers again.
[5] King Euija: Wine. / No. Don’t water it. I can tell when you water it.
[6] ── SCENE: The Hall ──
[7] ¶ The first man to say the obvious thing out loud is **Heungsu**. He says it smiling, the way he says everything.
[8] Heungsu: The Diamond Sutra says every made thing is like a dream, Majesty. A dewdrop. A flash of lightning. / Your new Assembly is a made thing.
[9] King Euija: Heungsu. Is this a sermon or a memorial?
[10] Heungsu: Both, Majesty. The sermon is free. / Bring the Satek and Yunbi men back to the benches before winter. If Silla comes, it comes over Tanhyeon. If Tang comes—
[11] King Euija: —it comes up the river. Yes. I can read a map. / You have a lovely voice, Heungsu. Gomamiji has nobody to hear it. Go and read them sutras.
[12] ¶ Euija calls it a temporary posting. The court knows better. The paper names a county far to the south: packed earth, a magistrate’s hut, and a long way from anyone who matters.
[13] ── SCENE: Gomamiji ──
[14] ¶ Gomamiji is a posting, not a retirement. He sits on the threshold until the dust on the hem looks like the hem. His office sword hangs on the doorpost. Nobody from Sabi writes.
[15] ── SCENE: The Banquet Hall ──
[16] ¶ He stops holding court. The wine comes earlier each day, and then it stops being tied to the day at all.
[17] ¶ Hundreds, by now. Nobody keeps the roll. They no longer have separate duties — only who pours, who steadies his wrist, who is still there when the wine runs out, and who is bold enough to speak while his mouth is busy elsewhere.
[18] ¶ The hems keep time better than the roll. A pour, a step, a kneel — the long court silk opens, and he watches that before he watches the wine.
[19] ¶ The feast is no longer a feast. The stories say three thousand. The room is not that. It is still too many, a harem so packed the lamp never finds a wall. Robes open early. The maids show him their bodies the way other courts show tribute, and he studies them the way he once studied a map.
[20] ¶ He is half-undressed by the second jar and does not bother to hide what the wine has done to him. They climb into his lap two at a time. They hike the silk and laugh when he looks. They toast until the lamps blur. On rainy nights the party spills out onto the night veranda, and he follows a hip down the night corridor as if it were the last order anyone will ever give him.
[21] ¶ Here is what the lamps do not show. The headband is gone, and nobody tells him to put it back on. The prince who could read a room in one glance cannot read past the next fold of silk. Every one of them flatters him. He knows it, and he likes knowing it. It is the only sum left in Sabi that always comes out in his favour.
[22] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. You said that yesterday, and again today. / …With the same breath on us. / The same teeth… at our collarbones.
[23] King Euija: Was it good? / Or… was it a good night.
[24] The Court Maids: …It was, yesterday. / The body still remembers. / Even if Your Majesty says stop… the hips answer first.
[25] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. Tell us about when you were young. / Before you… undo anything. / No — / While you undo it. / One word per knot.
[26] King Euija: …What is it you want to know.
[27] The Court Maids: They say you have more than fifty sons. / Samsin must keep a whole ledger just for Your Majesty. The kitchens have a wager going on how. / Nightly.
[28] King Euija: …That was the thirtieth Eraha. My father.
[29] The Court Maids: Ah. Then Your Majesty still has room to work with. / We can testify to it.
[30] The Court Maids: We knew already, in fairness. / Asking was only manners.
[31] ¶ He laughs for the first time in four months. It is the last recorded instance.
[32] ¶ Somewhere in the third year he stops going out to the hall, and some time after that they stop sending for him. The distance between those two things is the rest of the reign.
[33] ¶ Every season Chunbok asks the same question, in front of witnesses, the way a careful man pays a small tax. It buys him a name for loyalty. He already knows the answer.
[34] Satek Chunbok: Your Majesty…
[35] Satek Chunbok: Would it not be best to bring back General Gyebek?
[36] ¶ The letter is still in the king’s sleeve. It has gone soft at the folds.
[37] King Euija: That… who? / You there! Bring more wine!
[38] Baekje: Ahh~~ over here, Your Majesty~~
[39] The Court Maids: Your Majesty. The ministers are waiting outside.
[40] King Euija: …Let them wait.
[41] The Court Maids: Until when?
[42] King Euija: …
[43] ¶ He does not answer. After a while the question stops being asked, and after a while longer the ministers stop coming to the door. He notices none of it, and it is the first thing in his life he has not arranged on purpose.
[44] ¶ **Sungchung** comes while the wine is still being poured. He does not wait for a gap. He is the councillor who used to read the tides for the king, and he still wears his office sword as if there were an office.
[45] Sungchung: Your Majesty. Open court. Today.
[46] King Euija: We opened it. / With the cup.
[47] Sungchung: There is a tide. / If you miss it—
[48] ¶ He does not finish. The king is already on his feet.
[49] King Euija: Take his belt. / He wants open court? Give him a room where he can talk all day.
[50] ¶ The belt comes off in the aisle, and his rank goes with it. The guards walk him to a cell. After that, nobody else tries to speak.
[51] ── SCENE: The Cell ──
[52] ¶ **Sungchung** starves in a cell within earshot of the feast. His office sword hangs on the post outside. With the last of his ink he writes the king one page.
[53] ¶ In the cell where he starved, Kangrim reads his name three times — Sungchung. Sungchung. Sungchung. — loud enough for the feast next door to hear, or not hear.
[54] Kangrim: Councillor Sungchung. / You chose the cell over silence. Was that loyalty to the king — or loyalty to being right?
[55] Sungchung: …Being right is the only loyalty left when a king stops listening. / The paper is for him. Not for you.
[56] Kangrim: I will keep the minutes. Walk.
[57] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 16, dying memorial of Seongchung; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 384): A loyal servant does not forget his king even in death, so let me say one thing and die. I have always watched the times and studied their changes, and there will surely be war. Whoever uses soldiers must choose his ground with care: take the upper stream and draw the enemy to you, and you can keep the country whole. If foreign soldiers come, do not let them cross Chimhyeon by land, and do not let their ships into the banks of Final Ford. Hold the narrow, difficult places, and stop them there.❞
[58] ¶ The page reaches the banquet hall folded inside a guard’s glove. The king reads the first line. Then he sets it under a wine jar, and does not take it in.
[59] ¶ **Foxes in the Assembly. Toads in the treetops. A river running red. Nine signs, and a king who swears he doesn’t believe in signs…!**
